newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Inkatha ends boycott of constitution.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Inkatha ends boycott of constitution.

text.p: South Africa's opposition Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) said on Monday it had decided to end its 18-month boycott of the drafting of the country's final post-apartheid constitution.
"Our delegates are returning to the parliamentary sub- committees tomorrow (Tuesday)," senior Inkatha official Walter Felgate said in a telephone interview.
He said this did not amount to a decision to return to the full Constitutional Assembly, which is composed of all members of parliament.

The Zulu-based Inkatha, led by Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi, walked out of the assembly early last year in protest at the refusal of the ruling African National Congress to honour an agreement on international mediation over their differences.

The ANC and other parties carried on writing the constitution without the IFP, but earlier this month the constitutional court ruled that some aspects of the document they adopted in May would have to be redrafted.
Clauses referred back to the assembly by the court include those dealing with powers of provincial administrations, one of the main sticking points between Inkatha and the ANC.
Inkatha wants a great deal of autonomy for the provinces in a federal-type arrangement but the ANC wants the central government to wield most power.
ANC Secretary-General Cyril Ramaphosa, who is chairman of the Constitutional Assembly, has set October 7 as the deadline for finalisation of amendments in line with the court's 160-page judgment.

Felgate said that because of the deadline Inkatha delegates had to return to the two sub-committees drafting the amendments immediately or they would have no opportunity of making a meaningful contribution.
"Only our national council (of the party) can give us a mandate to return to the CA itself," he said. "We are looking at participating at least until the national council tells us otherwise."
Roelf Meyer, chief constitutional strategist for the National Party, the biggest opposition group, welcomed the Inkatha decision.
He said the plan was for the sub-committees to complete their work by October 7 and present the amendments to the Constitutional Assembly for ratification on October 11.
"Our view is that there is sufficient time, but that depends on the degree of cooperation all the parties show," Meyer said.
He said the Constitutional Court had indicated it needed to receive the amendments by the second week of October if it was to make a final judgment by the end of the year.
"All parties agree that it would be best to get it done by the end of the year," Meyer said.
